extracted.intended_audience: state environmental regulators, power sector owners/operators, industry stakeholders, and legal counsel participating in EPA CAA section 111 rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal/technical criteria used by EPA to identify the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER), define affected facilities/subcategories, set standards of performance (NSPS/EGUs), and evaluate applicability, cost-effectiveness, and technical feasibility for electric generating units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definition of 'standard of performance' (CAA §111)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The term ‘standard of performance’ means a standard for emissions of air pollutants which reflects the degree of emission limitation achievable through the application of the best system of emission reduction which (taking into account the cost of achieving such reduction and any nonair quality health and environmental impact and energy requirements) the Administrator determines has been adequately demonstrated.” 42 U.S.C. 7411(a)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When establishing standards, EPA must identify the BSER and the degree of emission limitation achievable through its application, considering cost, non-air quality health/environmental impacts, and energy requirements; EPA's determination must be based on what is 'adequately demonstrated.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for subcategorization based on operating horizon
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may create subcategories of designated facilities within a source category when many units share similar characteristics (including announced shorter operating horizons), and it is permissible for EPA to take operating horizon into account in determining the BSER for a subcategory of sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subcategorization is a tool within the BSER determination; states may still consider an individual unit's remaining useful life (RUL) for specific permitting decisions. If courts find EPA lacks authority to subcategorize based on retirement date, states could consider co-firing as alternative via remaining useful life considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: State consideration of remaining useful life (RUL) for individual sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 111(d) provides that, in applying standards of performance, a state may take into account, among other factors, the remaining useful life of a facility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision is intended to address exceptional circumstances at particular facilities; it does not prevent EPA from considering operating horizon for subcategorization at the category level. States can use RUL for particular units where unit-specific information differs from EPA's category-level analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER identification for certain sources: CCS with 90% capture
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA uses the phrase that BSER is CCS with 90 percent capture (and that CCS with 90 percent capture is achievable) interchangeably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the affected subcategory where EPA finds CCS achievable, the BSER is identified as application of CCS achieving ~90% capture; EPA's cost and feasibility assessments support that determination for the relevant sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-applicability of CCS to certain non-base load turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA proposed that because the BSER for non-base load combustion turbines was simple cycle technology, CCS was not applicable to those non-base load turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing applicability of CCS as BSER, EPA considers operational mode (base load vs. non-base load) and technology compatibility; CCS may be excluded where the BSER is demonstrated to be simple cycle operation for non-base load units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base load rating criterion (250 MMBtu/h)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA refers to the capability to combust 250 MMBtu/h of fossil fuel as the 'base load rating criterion' (equivalent to ~73 MW or 260 GJ/h heat input).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This numeric capacity threshold is used to classify units for applicability/subcategorization (i.e., what counts as base load-capable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of affected facility includes integrated auxiliary equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxiliary equipment such as boilers or combustion turbines that provide heat or electricity to the primary EGU (including to any control equipment) are considered integrated equipment and included as part of the affected facility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facility boundaries for performance standards should include integrated equipment that supports the primary EGU and any control equipment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approved methods for determining design efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTT lists 'ASME PTC 22 Gas Turbines,' 'ASME PTC 46 Overall Plant Performance,' and 'ISO 2314 Gas turbines—acceptance tests' as approved methods to determine the design efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design efficiency determinations submitted for applicability or compliance should use one of these approved test/measurement standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric-sales-based applicability and utilization thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Percent electric sales thresholds, capacity factor thresholds, and annual hours of operation limitations categorize combustion turbines based on utilization. EPA uses electric sales because the focus is facilities that sell electricity to the grid rather than on-site generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electric sales metrics determine whether a unit is treated as a grid-serving EGU for NSPS applicability; adjustments to design efficiency assumptions can materially change the electric sales threshold (e.g., using 3/4 of design efficiency halves the threshold impact).

rubrics_metrics.name: HHV/LHV conversion and reporting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The HHV of natural gas is 1.108 times the LHV; HHV efficiency = LHV efficiency divided by 1.108. Boiler efficiency in the U.S. is typically reported on an HHV basis; some regions (Europe) use LHV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing or converting efficiencies, use the 1.108 factor and be mindful of whether metrics/reporting are HHV- or LHV-based because thresholds and applicability calculations mix these bases (e.g., design efficiency caps on LHV but base load rating on HHV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design efficiency cap interplay with electric sales threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: While the design efficiency is capped at 50 percent on a LHV basis, the base load rating is on a HHV basis; this mixture results in the electric sales threshold being ~11 percent higher than the design efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy decisions about whether to base thresholds on design efficiency, HHV/LHV conventions, or adjusted design efficiency (e.g., 0.94×) affect applicability calculations; EPA solicited comment on basing the electric sales threshold on 0.94 times design efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower-emitting fuels definition for combustion turbines (≤160 lb CO2/MMBtu)
rubrics_metrics.description: For owners/operators of combustion turbines the lower emitting fuels requirement is defined to include fuels with an emissions rate of 160 lb CO2/MMBtu or less. For steam generating units or IGCC facilities the EPA requires the use of the maximum amount of non-coal fuels available to the affected facility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of fuels meeting ≤160 lb CO2/MMBtu demonstrates compliance for combustion turbines and is the BSER for multi-fuel-fired combustion turbines; steam/IGCC units must maximize non-coal fuel use as part of compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monthly site-specific fuel-based standards for co-firing turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: Combustion turbines co-firing natural gas with other fuels must determine fuel-based site-specific standards at the end of each operating month. The site-specific standards depend on the amount of co-fired natural gas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance accounting for co-fired units requires periodic (monthly) calculation of site-specific standards based on fuel mix; regulatory citations: 80 FR 64616 (Oct 23, 2015).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fuel-composition thresholds triggering multi-fuel subcategory (hydrogen co-firing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combustion turbines co-firing 25 percent hydrogen by volume could be subcategorized as multi-fuel-fired EGUs because the percent methane by volume could fall below 70 percent, the heating value could fall below 35 MJ/Sm3, and 10 percent of the heat input could be coming from a fuel not meeting the definition of natural gas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subcategorization may be based on quantifiable fuel-composition and heating-value thresholds that change the statutory classification of the unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-neutrality of standards (alternatives to CCS)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA recognizes that standards of performance are technology neutral and that a standard based on application of CCS could be achieved by co-firing hydrogen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a standard identifies an outcome (e.g., degree of emission limitation), regulated entities may achieve that outcome with different technologies or fuel strategies if they meet equivalent emission reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics minimizing low-load emissions for combustion turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: Important characteristics for minimizing emissions from low load combustion turbines include the ability to operate efficiently while operating at part load conditions and the ability to rapidly achieve maximum efficiency to minimize periods of operation at lower efficiencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and operational considerations (part-load efficiency and ramping behavior) matter for categorizing low-load units and setting appropriate BSER or subcategory standards; high steady-state design efficiency does not necessarily translate to good low-load performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effectiveness evaluation depends on key assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost effectiveness calculation is highly dependent upon assumptions concerning the increase in capital costs, the decrease in heat rate, and the price of natural gas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic reasonableness and cost-effectiveness determinations should disclose and test sensitivity to assumptions about capital costs, operational performance (heat rate), and fuel price trajectories; EPA used NETL baseline reports adjusted to 2022 dollars as inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of established technical and empirical evidence in feasibility judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA relied upon technical reports, operational experience (e.g., Boundary Dam, NETL analyses), vendor information, and demonstrated installations (including solvent technologies and capture approaches) to assess whether CCS or other systems are 'adequately demonstrated' and achievable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feasibility and 'adequately demonstrated' conclusions should cite commercial projects, peer-reviewed studies, DOE/NETL reports, and vendor performance data to support claims about technology maturity and expected performance.
